items.prompt: State what is meant by ethics for a computing professional.
items.canonical_answer: Ethics is the set of moral principles that guides how the professional acts: principles of honesty, care and responsibility that govern decisions the law alone does not reach.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - moral principles guiding the professional’s decisions where the law does not reach.

items.prompt: A young programmer in Windhoek joins the BCS as an associate member. Explain what the membership commits the programmer to, and what it signals.
items.canonical_answer: The membership commits the programmer to the BCS code of conduct: honest work, care for the public and for data, working within competence - a written standard for decisions the law does not reach. It signals to employers and clients that this programmer is held to a stated standard, with the body’s guidance to lean on when a decision is hard, so both sides of joining are the code and the signal.
marking_guidance: Context: this programmer’s joining of the given body - 1 mark for the commitment to the code of conduct.
Reason: because the body publishes the code and stands behind its members, the membership signals a standard, so employers and clients know what to hold the programmer to - 1 mark.

items.prompt: Describe two things a professional body such as the IEEE gives a computing professional.
items.canonical_answer: A published code of conduct: a written standard the member agrees to follow, so hard decisions have a rule to lean on. A community and standing: membership signals to employers and clients that the member works to that standard, and the body’s publications and meetings carry the profession’s knowledge, so the member is held to and helped by the same body.
marking_guidance: Features: two points, 1 mark each - the code of conduct with the standard it sets, and the standing and support the membership carries.

items.prompt: Explain why a computing professional needs a code of ethics beyond the law.
items.canonical_answer: The law sets a floor and reaches only so far: it forbids theft and misuse, but it says little about disclosing a system’s weaknesses, the care owed to users’ data or corner-cutting that harms no one yet. A code of ethics names those choices and sets a standard above the law’s floor, so hard decisions have a rule to lean on, which is why the professional needs more than the law.
marking_guidance: Reason: the law reaches only the floor, and much of the work’s ethics sits above it - 1 mark.
Purpose: so the professional has a written standard for the choices the law has not mapped, because data, money and safety are what the work touches - 1 mark.

objective_titles: Show understanding of the need for and purpose of ethics as a computing professional

items.prompt: State what is meant by acting ethically.
items.canonical_answer: Acting ethically is acting on moral principles - honesty, care, responsibility for the effects of the work - even where no rule forces the choice.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - acting on moral principles wherever the choice is not forced.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 7.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain the chain of impact when a developer unethically copies user data from a client’s system.
items.canonical_answer: The users’ personal data is taken without their consent, so their privacy is breached and their trust is broken; the client’s confidence in the developer collapses, so the client’s business loses a working relationship and warns others; and the developer’s and the profession’s reputation falls, so every professional meets harder questions. One act, three circles of damage - the users, the client, the profession - which is why the impact runs past the act itself.
marking_guidance: Change: the unethical copying - 1 mark - so the effect on people is breached privacy and broken trust, because the data was taken without consent.
Consequence: the damage spreads to the client and the profession, so the result is lost confidence and a spent reputation, which is what the chain adds to the single act - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 7.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Show understanding of the need to act ethically and the impact of acting ethically or unethically for a given situation

items.prompt: A software house finds a safety flaw in a hospital system it supports. The contract says nothing about telling anyone. Explain the ethical course and the impact of taking it.
items.canonical_answer: The ethical course is disclosure: the hospital is told at once and in detail, and the flaw is mended, because the patients’ safety comes before the contract’s silence. The impact of acting ethically is trust - the flaw is fixed before harm, the hospital keeps faith with the house, and the profession’s standing is upheld - so the disclosure costs some embarrassment and buys the safety of the people the system serves, which is the impact that matters.
marking_guidance: Context: this house with its given contract silence - 1 mark for the ethical course named with its reason.
Reason: because patients’ safety outranks the contract’s silence, disclosure and mending buy trust and prevent harm, so the impact of the ethical act is what the answer traces - 1 mark.

items.prompt: Describe two impacts of ethical behaviour by a computing professional.
items.canonical_answer: Trust: users supply honest data and rely on the systems, because a professional known for care is believed, so the work carries weight. Standing: the profession keeps its reputation, because one careless act is remembered against all professionals, so ethical behaviour protects the standing every professional depends on.
marking_guidance: Features: two impacts as two points, 1 mark each - the trust the work earns, and the profession’s standing the behaviour protects.

items.prompt: Explain why unethical behaviour by one professional damages more than that one person.
items.canonical_answer: The act lands on people - leaked data breaches privacy, a careless system fails its users - and it lands on the profession: the public meets computing through its professionals, and one misused trust is remembered against all of them, so the next professional meets harder questions. The standing the profession built is spent by the one who broke it, which is why codes bind individuals for a collective’s sake.
marking_guidance: Reason: the act harms the people the work touches, and the public keeps one memory for all professionals - 1 mark.
Purpose: so the profession polices its own standing, because a spent reputation is paid for by every member - 1 mark.

items.prompt: State what copyright legislation gives the creator of a work.
items.canonical_answer: Copyright gives the creator the legal right to control how the work is copied, adapted and distributed: the work belongs to its maker unless the right is assigned away.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - the legal right to control copying, adapting and distribution of the work.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 7.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Show understanding of the need for copyright legislation

items.prompt: A small studio in Swakopmund sells its game online and finds copies being shared freely. Explain what copyright legislation lets the studio do.
items.canonical_answer: The studio owns the game’s copyright, so copying and sharing it without permission is against the studio’s right to refuse: the legislation lets the studio demand the copying stop, pursue payment for copies already taken and take action against the sharers. Without that right, the studio’s work could be taken and sold by anyone, which is the need the law answers for a maker of any size.
marking_guidance: Context: this studio and its freely shared game - 1 mark for what the right allows: stop, claim, act.
Reason: because copyright gives the maker control of copying, the studio can refuse and pursue the sharers, so the right is what the studio leans on - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 7.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Show understanding of the need for copyright legislation

items.prompt: A learner writes that copyright means copying someone’s work without permission. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: That is breaking copyright, not what copyright is. Copyright is the legal right of the creator to control copying and use of their work; plagiarism and copying without permission are acts against that right. The test: is the answer about the right, or about breaking it? Copyright is the right; the breach has other names.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the breach of the right has been given as the right’s definition, a confusion of the two.
1 mark: the correction with the test - copyright is the maker’s right to control copying, while copying without permission breaks it.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 7.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Show understanding of the need for copyright legislation

items.prompt: Describe two reasons why copyright legislation is needed for software.
items.canonical_answer: Software can be copied exactly at almost no cost, so without the right to control copying, a creator’s work could be taken and sold by anyone and creating would stop paying. And software is skilled work over time - design, code, testing - so the law protects that investment the way it protects a book or a song, which is why the maker’s right reaches software too.
marking_guidance: Features: two reasons as two points, 1 mark each - the cheapness of exact copying, and the protection of the work’s investment.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 7.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Show understanding of the need for copyright legislation

items.prompt: Explain why copyright matters to a lone developer as much as to a large firm.
items.canonical_answer: Copyright belongs to the creator, whatever the creator’s size: a lone developer’s program is as much their work as a firm’s, and the lone developer has less behind them to absorb the loss. The right to control copying is what lets a small maker sell their work, so the law a firm can lean on is the law a lone developer lives by, which is why it matters to both.
marking_guidance: Reason: the right belongs to the maker at any size, and the small maker has less to absorb a loss - 1 mark.
Purpose: so the lone developer can sell their work on the same footing, because control of copying is what selling rests on - 1 mark.

objective_titles: Show understanding of the need for copyright legislation

items.prompt: Explain one benefit to a school of using free software (Free Software Foundation) for its administration system.
items.canonical_answer: The licence gives the freedom to run, study, change and share the source code, so the school can adapt the system to its own ways of working, share its improvements with other schools, and have anyone it trusts inspect the code - and no licence fee is charged for any of it. The benefit is freedom plus cost: the school owns its system’s behaviour rather than renting it.
marking_guidance: Benefit: the freedom to study, change and share the source - 1 mark.
Because the licence guarantees those freedoms and charges no fee, the school adapts and inspects at will, so the system is the school’s own - 1 mark.

objective_titles: Show understanding of the different types of software licencing and justify the use of a licence for a given situation

items.prompt: Explain one drawback to a small business of using open-source software for a critical system.
items.canonical_answer: No one is contractually obliged to mend it: faults are fixed by the community or by the business itself, so a critical fault on a deadline may wait for a volunteer, and the business needs its own skills to adapt and maintain the code. The licence allows the work, but the responsibility for the work sits with whoever uses it, which is the small business’s own desk.
marking_guidance: Drawback: no contractual maintainer, so faults wait on the community or the business - 1 mark.
Because the licence leaves the maintenance to its user, a small business without those skills inherits the desk, so the critical system rests on its own competence - 1 mark.

objective_titles: Show understanding of the different types of software licencing and justify the use of a licence for a given situation

items.prompt: A club wants a website its keen programmers can restyle and extend, and its budget is small; a firm wants its payroll system supported, maintained and held to a contract. Explain which licence type suits each, and why.
items.canonical_answer: The club should choose free or open-source software: the source is available and may be changed and shared, so the keen programmers restyle and extend the site themselves, with no licence fee weighing on the small budget. The firm should choose commercial software: the vendor supplies support and maintenance under a contract, so a fault at month end is the vendor’s paid problem, which is what a payroll demands. Each choice follows from who can maintain the system and who must answer for it, which is the justification.
marking_guidance: Suitable choices named for both situations - 1 mark for the club’s open licence, because the programmers and the budget suit changeable source.
Reason for the firm: a commercial contract makes the vendor answerable, so the payroll’s maintenance is guaranteed - 1 mark.
Context: the justification is developed in this scenario - who maintains and who answers is what decides each - 1 mark.

objective_titles: Show understanding of the different types of software licencing and justify the use of a licence for a given situation

items.prompt: A learner writes that free software just means software free of charge. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Free of charge is freeware: software given away without the right to see or change the source. Free software, in the Free Software Foundation’s sense, gives the freedom to run, study, change and share the source code, whatever it costs - the word names freedom, not a price. The test: can you see and change the source code? Then it is free software, not just freeware.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - free of charge has been taken as the meaning of ‘free’, a confusion of freeware with free software.
1 mark: the correction with the test - free software guarantees the freedoms to run, study, change and share the source, which freeware does not.

items.prompt: Explain why an organisation might choose commercial software for a critical system rather than open-source.
items.canonical_answer: Critical systems need someone answerable: commercial software comes with a vendor’s contract - support, maintenance, agreed response - so a fault at month end is the vendor’s paid problem, with people whose job it is. Open-source leaves the maintenance to the organisation’s own skills or the community’s goodwill, so the organisation must be able to do the work itself, which a critical system should not rest on alone.

items.prompt: Describe the difference between free software and open-source software.
items.canonical_answer: Both make the source available and allow change and sharing, whereas the difference is the stance: free software (Free Software Foundation) puts the user’s freedom first as a matter of principle, treating the freedoms to run, study, change and share as rights; open-source software (Open Source Initiative) presents similar practical terms as a way of building good software, emphasising the method over the principle. The licences overlap in practice, so the philosophies are what differ.
marking_guidance: Difference: rights-as-principle against method-for-quality - 1 mark for each side, whereas both allow change and sharing, and both sides are needed.

items.prompt: Explain why AI raises ethical questions for a computing professional.
items.canonical_answer: AI systems make judgements that affect people - who gets flagged, what a diagnosis suggests, whose face a camera names - and a judgement made by a system is still a professional’s act somewhere, so responsibility does not disappear into the software. The data a system learns from carries its own bias and its own privacy, so the professional must ask both whether the system works and whom it works on, which is why AI raises ethics and not only engineering.
marking_guidance: Reason: the system’s judgements affect people, and the professional owns the act - 1 mark.
Purpose: so the questions asked include fairness and privacy of the data, because engineering alone is not what AI asks of a professional - 1 mark.

items.prompt:
A youth radio station in Rundu is building its website. A volunteer finds a slick gallery script on another site, whose footer reads "All rights reserved", and copies it into the station’s code. The station also begins using an AI voice assistant to read the hourly news.
(a) Explain what copyright says about the volunteer’s copying of the gallery script, and what the station should do. [3]
(b) Explain one impact on the station of acting ethically here, and one impact of acting unethically. [3]
(c) Explain one ethical question the station should ask itself about the AI voice reading the news. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The script belongs to its creator, and "all rights reserved" means the right to copy and adapt has not been given away, so copying it into the station’s site is against the creator’s right. The station should remove the copied code, ask the creator for a licence or write its own gallery, because the maker’s permission is what the law requires.
(b) Acting ethically, the station earns trust: the volunteer writes an honest site and its donors and listeners keep faith with a station that respects makers, so the station’s name is safe. Acting unethically, the station risks a takedown demand, a claim for damages and a public story about a station that steals code, so its name is spent.
(c) Does the audience know the voice is a system’s, and is the reading answerable when it is wrong? A synthetic voice reading real news makes the station responsible for what it reads out, so the station should ask who answers for an error the AI reads as fact.
marking_guidance: Part (a): the reason the copying is against the maker’s right - 3 marks, 1 per point: the reserved rights, the breach, the remedy of licensing or writing its own.
Part (b): the context of this station’s choice - 3 marks, 1 per point: the trust earned ethically, the demand and damages risked, the public story that spends the name.
Part (c): the ethical question named with its reason - 2 points: the audience’s knowing, the answerability of the synthetic reading.

context.situation: A radio station builds a site with copied code and an AI news voice.
